name: Deep Space 2
intro: Deep Space 2 was a pair of small test probes, named Amundsen and Scott, that rode to Mars on Mars Polar Lander. On 3 December 1999 they were meant to smash into the ground near the south pole and test the soil for water, but no signal ever came back. The see-through shapes show one probe and its shell at real size.
whyLeft: They were built to hit the ground and stay there. Nobody knows what went wrong, because no signal was ever received; a review found they had not been tested enough before launch.
repurpose: Nothing is known to fix, and their exact spot is unknown. A future orbiter with a sharp camera could search for their tiny holes, and the idea of crash-landing probes is still studied for other worlds.

hotspots.title: The impact hole
hotspots.text: Each probe was built to hit the ground at about 200 meters a second, faster than 700 km/h, and bury itself like a dart. Nobody knows whether they survived the hit.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: Mars Polar Lander and Deep Space 2 landing sites

hotspots.title: The buried half
hotspots.text: Each probe was planned to split in two. The front half would dig up to about 60 cm into the ground, still connected by a cable to the back half at the surface.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: Mars Polar Lander and Deep Space 2 landing sites

hotspots.title: The back half
hotspots.text: The back half stayed at the surface with the antenna. It was meant to radio its findings up to Mars Global Surveyor in orbit, which never heard a thing.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: Mars Polar Lander and Deep Space 2 landing sites

hotspots.title: Scott’s twin
hotspots.text: The two probes, Amundsen and Scott, were named after the explorers who raced to Earth’s South Pole. They came down somewhere near Mars Polar Lander’s target, but their exact spots are unknown.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: Mars Polar Lander and Deep Space 2 landing sites

hotspots.title: A shell made to shatter
hotspots.text: Each probe rode inside a shell 35 centimeters across, a little bigger than a basketball. Its shape kept it falling nose-first, and the shell was made to shatter when it hit the ground.

photo.alt: A worker in a white clean-room suit and hair net leans over a small red cone-shaped probe on a stand, marked with a fragile sticker.
photo.caption: A Jet Propulsion Laboratory worker checks one of the Deep Space 2 probes in Florida in November 1998, before launch.

hotspots.title: A tiny drill
hotspots.text: A tiny drill was to poke out of the buried half and pull a pinch of soil inside. A heater would warm the soil, and a laser would look for water vapor coming off it.

source.label: NASA JPL: Deep Space 2 sample collection and water experiment

hotspots.title: Tough batteries
hotspots.text: The probes’ batteries were specially made to live through the crash. In a test of an early version, they survived a jolt 45,000 times stronger than gravity.

source.label: NASA JPL: Mars penetrators complete crucial subsystem test

funFact: Each probe, inside its protective shell, was small enough to carry in your arms, and it was dropped without a parachute, on purpose.

source.label: Estimate; the probes were built to bury themselves up to 0.6 m deep, and were never found (NSSDCA)
